record.question: Under the Baltimore City Employees' Retirement Systems (BCERS) alternatives consultant RFP, what must the consultant's quarterly performance report include at a minimum?
record.answer:
# Markdown Briefing: BCERS Quarterly Performance Report Minimum Requirements

Under the **Baltimore City Employees' Retirement Systems (BCERS) Alternatives Consultant RFP**, the consultant’s **quarterly performance report** must include, at a minimum:

## Required Contents
1. **Market overview and outlook**
2. **Allocation breakdown** by:
   - geography
   - strategy
   - industry
3. **An update on each fund**
4. **A listing of each fund by strategy**
5. **Date of commitment** to each fund
6. **Commitment amount** to each fund
7. **Drawdown amounts** by fund
8. **Outstanding commitment** by fund
9. **Distribution amounts** by fund
10. **Fund net asset values (NAVs)**
11. **IRR and multiples** for each fund

## Required Aggregate Reporting
Items **6 through 11** must also be aggregated for:
- the **core private equity portfolio**
- the **specialized portfolio**
- the **total portfolio** (**core + specialized**)

## Source Context
These requirements appear in the RFP’s **“Reporting Requirements”** section under **“Quarterly performance report to include at a minimum.”**

Under the BCERS Alternatives Consultant RFP, the consultant’s quarterly performance report must include, at a minimum:

1. Market overview and outlook.
2. Allocation breakdown by geography, strategy, and industry.
3. An update on each fund.
4. A listing of each fund by strategy.
5. The date of commitment to each fund.
6. The commitment amount to each fund.
7. Drawdown amounts by fund.
8. Outstanding commitment by fund.
9. Distribution amounts by fund.
10. Fund net asset values.
11. IRR and multiples of each fund.
12. Items 6 through 11 aggregated for:
   - the core private equity portfolio,
   - the specialized portfolio, and
   - the total portfolio (core and specialized).

These requirements appear in the RFP’s “Reporting Requirements” section under “Quarterly performance report to include at a minimum.”

SECTION I: Background & Nature of Services Required
This section contains important information covering the Baltimore City Employees’ Retirement 
System (“ERS”) as well as the Retiree Benefit Trust (“OPEB Trust”) and the proposal process for 
selecting an Alternatives Consultant. For the purpose of this RFP, the Employees’ Retirement System
and the OPEB Trust will be referred to as Baltimore City Employees' Retirement Systems (“BCERS”).
A. Introduction
The BCERS is soliciting proposals for a full-service professional Alternatives Consultant, on a 
non-discretionary basis, with broad investment expertise and service capabilities to assist the 
Board and work operationally with the BCERS staff. The Board will be contracting with only 
one investment firm to assist with the alternative investment management of the BCERS.
B. BCERS 
The Employees' Retirement System was established January 1, 1926, by City Ordinance 
as contained in Article 22 of the Baltimore City Code. It is a contributory, defined benefit local 
government retirement plan that provides service retirement, disability and death benefits to 
non-uniformed employees of the City of Baltimore, and to the survivors and beneficiaries of 
such employees. In 2024, members' contributions were 5% of pay. As of June 30, 2024, total 
ERS membership was 17,869.
The OPEB Trust was established in 2007 by the City, in response to the Governmental 
Accounting Standards Board Statement Numbers 43 and 45, to pre-fund retiree healthcare 
and other post-employment benefits (“OPEB Trust”).
As a fiduciary body, the BCERS Board has responsibility for managing and investing the funds 
of the ERS and the OPEB Trust. 
BCERS is governed by a single nine (9) member Board of Trustees comprised of: two ex-officio members; two members appointed by the Mayor; two additional members appointed 
by the Mayor, subject to recommendations made by the President of City Council; two trustees
elected by the active members of the ERS System; and one trustee elected by the retired 
members of the ERS System. Appointed and elected trustees each serve a four-year term. 
Appointed trustees continue to serve until replaced by the Mayor or until the expiration of two 
consecutive full terms. The members of the Board, in conjunction with the Executive Director 
determine policies and make investment decisions concerning the administrative and 
investment operations of the BCERS. 
C. Investment Program
Please refer to the BCERS' Statement of Investment Objectives, Policies and Guidelines, for 
information on the investment program, as outlined in the Board of Trustees Governance 
Manual posted on our website: https://www.bcers.org/publications/governance-manual/
The investment managers for ERS are contained in the Annual Comprehensive Financial 
Report (ACFR) posted on our website:
https://www.bcers.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ERS-ACFR-LowRes.pdf

 D. Scope of Service
Under the direction of the Board of Trustees, and staff, the Alternatives Consultant will 
provide comprehensive, full-retainer, alternatives consulting advice and services to include 
Private Equity. Specifically, the successful firm will demonstrate superior experience and 
capability in the area of alternative investments, with primary responsibility for an 
appropriately structured private equity program. 
Please note that BCERS currently retains a separate general investment consultant, Marquette 
Associates, Inc., that assists with strategic and tactical investment planning, asset allocation, 
market research, investment due diligence, portfolio monitoring, performance measurements

and reporting. The role of the general consultant included all asset classes until 2017, when 
the Alternatives Consultant was initially hired. 
The following are examples of the duties the BCERS expect the Alternatives Consultant to 
perform.
(1) Private Equity Oversight Duties:
• Assist the BCERS Board of Trustees (Board) and BCERS staff in the development of 
appropriately structured private equity programs; assist with the establishment of goals, 
strategies, objectives and performance standards.
• Develop a structured, ongoing process to screen the global universe of available private 
equity investments (i.e., U.S. and non-U.S. opportunities) and identify those most 
appropriate for BCERS portfolios; provide necessary reports summarizing screening 
activity.
• Evaluate prospective investments, including those that may be sourced by BCERS staff. If 
appropriate, engage in comprehensive due diligence that may include general partner site 
visits, background and reference checking.
• Present written investment recommendation reports to the Board and BCERS staff; 
reports will include, but shall not be limited to, full results of the comprehensive due 
diligence, strategic considerations, partnership reviews, commitment amounts and how 
the investments complement the overall portfolio.
• Work with BCERS staff and legal counsel to negotiate, in the best interests of BCERS, 
relevant contracts and legal documents including, but not limited to, limited partnership 
agreements, side letters, and subscription agreements.
• Coordinate and communicate with BCERS and other BCERS consultants and advisors as 
appropriate to ensure effective administration of the private equity programs.
• Provide on-going investment monitoring that may include attending annual meetings, 
analyzing policy and peer benchmarks, and conducting manager meetings. 
• Provide regular updates/assessments of relevant operational and/or strategic changes 
with investment managers, including, but not limited to, performance, organization, 
ownership, investment products, and disclosure issues.
• Review and recommend course of action on all fund documents, consents and extensions. 
Ensure that investments comply with the terms of their contracts.
• Assist and advise BCERS staff with work-out situations, breaches or violations of limited 
partnership and side letter provisions, and fund dissolutions as may arise.
(2) Policy Duties:
• Provide recommendations concerning and assist with developing investment goals, 
policies, guidelines and procedures for private equity publicly managed portfolios.

E. Minimum Qualifications
A proposing firm (Proposer) must meet all of the following minimum qualifications to BCERS'

• The firm must have been in business for at least seven (7) or more years providing general

• The firm must be directly responsible for the management of the account, and all 
personnel responsible for the account must be employees of the firm.
• Must currently serve as consultant for at least five pension funds each with aggregate 
assets over $1.5 billion in the public funds, endowment, or corporate pension fund 
markets. Must also consult for clients with private equity investment programs of at least 
10% of total assets.
• The primary consultant assigned to the BCERS relationship must have a minimum of five 
(5) years of consulting experience with defined benefit public pension plans, and have 
been employed by the firm for at least three (3) years. 
• Serve as a fiduciary to the Board and acknowledge in writing to comply with the Board’s 
Investment Policies and Guidelines.

SECTION I: Background & Nature of Services Required
This section contains important information covering the Baltimore City Employees’ Retirement 
System (“ERS”) as well as the Retiree Benefit Trust (“OPEB Trust”) and the proposal process for 
selecting an Alternatives Consultant. For the purpose of this RFP, the Employees’ Retirement System
and the OPEB Trust will be referred to as Baltimore City Employees' Retirement Systems (“BCERS”).
A. Introduction
The BCERS is soliciting proposals for a full-service professional Alternatives Consultant, on a 
non-discretionary basis, with broad investment expertise and service capabilities to assist the 
Board and work operationally with the BCERS staff. The Board will be contracting with only 
one investment firm to assist with the alternative investment management of the BCERS.
B. BCERS 
The Employees' Retirement System was established January 1, 1926, by City Ordinance 
as contained in Article 22 of the Baltimore City Code. It is a contributory, defined benefit local 
government retirement plan that provides service retirement, disability and death benefits to 
non-uniformed employees of the City of Baltimore, and to the survivors and beneficiaries of 
such employees. In 2024, members' contributions were 5% of pay. As of June 30, 2024, total 
ERS membership was 17,869.
The OPEB Trust was established in 2007 by the City, in response to the Governmental 
Accounting Standards Board Statement Numbers 43 and 45, to pre-fund retiree healthcare 
and other post-employment benefits (“OPEB Trust”).
As a fiduciary body, the BCERS Board has responsibility for managing and investing the funds 
of the ERS and the OPEB Trust. 
BCERS is governed by a single nine (9) member Board of Trustees comprised of: two ex-officio members; two members appointed by the Mayor; two additional members appointed 
by the Mayor, subject to recommendations made by the President of City Council; two trustees
elected by the active members of the ERS System; and one trustee elected by the retired 
members of the ERS System. Appointed and elected trustees each serve a four-year term. 
Appointed trustees continue to serve until replaced by the Mayor or until the expiration of two 
consecutive full terms. The members of the Board, in conjunction with the Executive Director 
determine policies and make investment decisions concerning the administrative and 
investment operations of the BCERS. 
C. Investment Program
Please refer to the BCERS' Statement of Investment Objectives, Policies and Guidelines, for 
information on the investment program, as outlined in the Board of Trustees Governance 
Manual posted on our website: https://www.bcers.org/publications/governance-manual/
The investment managers for ERS are contained in the Annual Comprehensive Financial 
Report (ACFR) posted on our website:
https://www.bcers.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ERS-ACFR-LowRes.pdf

Investment Consultant Services: Requests for Proposal 3 of 37
Instructions
Orange County Employees Retirement System (“OCERS”) is requesting proposals from qualified firms 
interested in providing pension fund investment consulting services that will help OCERS improve portfolio 
performance over the long run while managing risk in alignment with the risk profiles articulated collectively 
by our Investment Committee. The primary objectives are to provide OCERS with non-discretionary consulting 
services for the entire OCERS’ portfolio or any one or combination of the following services:
General investments and total portfolio risk
Private equity investments
Real assets investments
Real estate investments
The specific services requested via this Request for Proposal (“RFP”) are contained in Section 2: Description of 
Services Sought and Appendix “D”: Scope of Services.
Step 1: Submit Intent to Respond
If your firm is interested in responding to this RFP, please submit your Intent to Respond (Appendix “A”), via 
email to the Point of Contact identified in Section 4, by 5:00 p.m., PT, September 10, 2021. Failure to submit 
your Intent to Respond may disqualify your firm from submitting a response to this RFP.
Step 2: Submit Questions
Questions about this RFP must be submitted in writing to the Point of Contact by 5:00 pm, PT, September 10, 
2021. All questions received and responses thereto will be posted on OCERS’s website before 5:00 pm, PT, 
September 20, 2021.
Step 3: Submit Response
Those who wish to be considered must submit their completed proposal, via email to the Point of Contact, by 
5:00 p.m., PT, October 1, 2021. Any proposal delivered after the proposal deadline will not be considered.
Respondents are invited to submit proposals for any one, combination, or all of the Investments Consulting 
Services listed above. Respondents must clearly indicate which consultant service(s) your firm intends to offer
using the checklist provided in the Proposal Cover Page and Checklist (Appendix “B”). Specific instructions for 
proposal submissions are contained in Section 6: Proposal Requirements of this RFP.

Investment Consultant Services: Requests for Proposal 4 of 37
Section 1: Background
OCERS was established in 1945 under the provisions of the County Employees Retirement Law of 1937, and 
provides members with retirement, disability, death, and cost-of-living benefits. There are approximately 
42,000 members served by OCERS, of which over 15,000 are retirees. OCERS is governed by a ten-member 
Board of Retirement (“Board”) which has plenary authority and fiduciary responsibility for investment of 
monies and administration of the retirement system. The OCERS Investment Committee is comprised of all the 
members of the Board. OCERS has over ninety employees and the Board appoints a Chief Executive Officer 
who is responsible for the management of the agency. 
The OCERS’ investment portfolio, approximately $21.5 billion in assets as of June 30, 2021, is diversified 
globally and across multiple asset classes. Currently OCERS’ contributions from members and employers are 
largely sufficient to fund the retiree payrolls. OCERS invests in separate accounts, commingled vehicles, funds 
of one, funds of funds, limited partnerships, and co-investments through external investment managers. The 
Investment Committee has delegated to the Chief Investment Officer (CIO) the responsibility to manage the 
investment portfolio subject to Investment Committee approved policies. Further details on OCERS’
Investment Portfolio, asset allocation as well as website links to the Investment Policy Statement, current 
consultant reports, and actuarial information are attached as Appendix “C” (OCERS’ Investment Portfolio).

without qualification. The Consultant will work with OCERS’ Investment Team on assigned duties and projects 
as an extension of OCERS’ team and reliable research provider. The CIO coordinates the activities of the 
Consultant under general direction from the Investment Committee. In all cases, the Consultant and its 
representatives shall offer advice that is solely in the interest of OCERS and perform its duties in accordance 
with the OCERS’ investment guidelines.

advice, conduct asset allocation study, manage total portfolio risk, report and monitor the entire portfolio, 
conduct due diligence, collaborate with OCERS’ Investment Team and Investment Committee, and attend

alternative assets portfolio, collaborate with OCERS’ Investment Team and Investment Committee, and attend 
meetings as needed.

Asset Class Objective and Goals:
• Global Public Equity
The investment objective of the global equity is to achieve consistent positive real returns and to 
maximize long-term total return with prudent levels of risk through a combination of income and 
capital appreciation. OCERS has adopted a style diversified structure that is designed to have 
aggregate equity portfolio characteristics similar to that of the global equity market as represented by 
the MSCI ACWI IMI Index. While passive management is utilized in the more efficient parts of the 
markets, active management is favored for small cap, emerging market equity, etc.
• Private Equity
The objective of the private equity asset class is to provide diversification for the overall portfolio and 
enhance returns; a diversified global portfolio targeting top-quartile managers within each segment of 
the market. The asset class is composed of fund of funds, direct private equity, and non-performing 
and/or equity-like private credit. The asset class is targeting 63% buyout, 25% venture, 7% special 
situations, and 5% other (non-core interests through legacy FoFs); and 64% North America, 20% 
Europe, 13% Asia, and 3% Global. Additionally, 10% of the annual private equity commitments are set 
aside for co-investment opportunities alongside OCERS’ current existing GP relationships. 
OCERS will continue to seek out direct fund investments in top-quartile managers globally. Private 
equity has a pacing plan to deploy $675 million in 2021 and $700 million in 2022. OCERS will also focus 
on top-quartile managers that will provide co-investment opportunities, allowing OCERS to top up on 
“best ideas” while bringing down the total fee load. Co-investments with existing and approved 
General Partners in sizes of $5 to $10 million are approved under the current guidelines.
• Fixed Income
The objective of the fixed income asset class is to diversify equity risk, preserve capital, generate 
income, and in the case of TIPS, protect against inflation. The asset class is broken down into two main 
categories: investment grade bonds and TIPS. The former is mostly actively managed through core and 
core-plus mandates. TIPS are invested in an index fund. 
• Credit
The objective of this asset class is to allow the plan to capture the credit risk premium. Credit has a 7% 
overall target in the portfolio and includes four main sub-asset classes: corporate credit, opportunistic 
credit, emerging markets debt, and performing bond-like private credit. The asset class is targeting 
35% corporate credit and opportunistic credit, 29% emerging markets debt, and 36% private credit.
The corporate credit allocation is made up of corporate bonds and banks loans that are mainly below 
investment grade. Opportunistic credit seeks to deliver returns by taking advantage of periods of 
credit dislocation in public markets. OCERS’ emerging markets debt exposure is predominantly 
expressed through blended mandates in local and external emerging markets sovereign debt. Finally, 
the majority of the private credit exposure is in middle market direct lending and asset based lending.
As for the private credit sub-asset class, it has a pacing plan to deploy $125 to $200 million per year 
across 2 to 3 investments.
• Real Assets: 
The objective of the real assets asset class is to provide diversification for the overall portfolio while 
providing income and an inflation hedge. Real assets has a 5% overall target in the portfolio and 
includes infrastructure, energy, timber, agriculture, and other hard asset strategies. 
Real assets has a pacing plan to deploy $100 to $150 million per year across 2 to 3 investments.

Investment Consultant Services: Requests for Proposal 16 of 37
• Real Estate
Within real estate, OCERS targets 60% to core strategies and 40% to non-core strategies with up to 
10% of the real estate allocation permitted to be invested in non-U.S. assets. OCERS will continue to 
move towards a balance of core and non-core real estate investment allocations.
• Risk Mitigation
The objective of the risk mitigation asset class includes protecting against an equity market decline, 
diversifying the total portfolio away from growth risk, and having a positive return over a cycle. The 
asset class is composed of 25% target allocation each to long-term treasuries, global macro, 
systematic trend following, and alternative risk premia. 
• Unique Strategies
The objective of the unique strategies asset class is to enhance return and diversify the risks of the 
OCERS’ portfolio while exhibiting a low correlation to public equity and fixed income markets. This 
portion of the portfolio is reserved for strategies that are truly unique and while differentiated from 
those in the portfolio’s other main asset classes, can have characteristics of multiple or overlapping 
asset classes but are not easily categorized by just one in particular. For this reason, Unique Strategies 
may fall under the purview of any OCERS’ Investment Consultant.
Since there is no target for Unique Strategies, the category will continue to be utilized in an 
opportunistic manner and will continue to evolve over time, likely increasing the OCERS’ portfolio 
exposure to new and niche platforms and strategies in the future.

Instructions
Orange County Employees Retirement System (“OCERS”) is requesting proposals from qualified firms 
interested in providing pension fund investment consulting services that will help OCERS improve portfolio 
performance over the long run while managing risk in alignment with the risk profiles articulated collectively 
by our Investment Committee. The primary objectives are to provide OCERS with non-discretionary consulting 
services for the entire OCERS’ portfolio or any one or combination of the following services:
General investments and total portfolio risk
Private equity investments
Real assets investments
Real estate investments
The specific services requested via this Request for Proposal (“RFP”) are contained in Section 2: Description of 
Services Sought and Appendix “D”: Scope of Services.
Step 1: Submit Intent to Respond
If your firm is interested in responding to this RFP, please submit your Intent to Respond (Appendix “A”), via 
email to the Point of Contact identified in Section 4, by 5:00 p.m., PT, September 10, 2021. Failure to submit 
your Intent to Respond may disqualify your firm from submitting a response to this RFP.
Step 2: Submit Questions
Questions about this RFP must be submitted in writing to the Point of Contact by 5:00 pm, PT, September 10, 
2021. All questions received and responses thereto will be posted on OCERS’s website before 5:00 pm, PT, 
September 20, 2021.
Step 3: Submit Response
Those who wish to be considered must submit their completed proposal, via email to the Point of Contact, by 
5:00 p.m., PT, October 1, 2021. Any proposal delivered after the proposal deadline will not be considered.
Respondents are invited to submit proposals for any one, combination, or all of the Investments Consulting 
Services listed above. Respondents must clearly indicate which consultant service(s) your firm intends to offer
using the checklist provided in the Proposal Cover Page and Checklist (Appendix “B”). Specific instructions for 
proposal submissions are contained in Section 6: Proposal Requirements of this RFP.

Investment Consultant Services: Requests for Proposal 4 of 37
Section 1: Background
OCERS was established in 1945 under the provisions of the County Employees Retirement Law of 1937, and 
provides members with retirement, disability, death, and cost-of-living benefits. There are approximately 
42,000 members served by OCERS, of which over 15,000 are retirees. OCERS is governed by a ten-member 
Board of Retirement (“Board”) which has plenary authority and fiduciary responsibility for investment of 
monies and administration of the retirement system. The OCERS Investment Committee is comprised of all the 
members of the Board. OCERS has over ninety employees and the Board appoints a Chief Executive Officer 
who is responsible for the management of the agency. 
The OCERS’ investment portfolio, approximately $21.5 billion in assets as of June 30, 2021, is diversified 
globally and across multiple asset classes. Currently OCERS’ contributions from members and employers are 
largely sufficient to fund the retiree payrolls. OCERS invests in separate accounts, commingled vehicles, funds 
of one, funds of funds, limited partnerships, and co-investments through external investment managers. The 
Investment Committee has delegated to the Chief Investment Officer (CIO) the responsibility to manage the 
investment portfolio subject to Investment Committee approved policies. Further details on OCERS’
Investment Portfolio, asset allocation as well as website links to the Investment Policy Statement, current 
consultant reports, and actuarial information are attached as Appendix “C” (OCERS’ Investment Portfolio).
For additional information about OCERS, please refer to the OCERS website at ocers.org.
Section 2: Description of Services Sought
The Investment Consultant will serve in a fiduciary capacity and will acknowledge in writing its fiduciary status, 
without qualification. The Consultant will work with OCERS’ Investment Team on assigned duties and projects 
as an extension of OCERS’ team and reliable research provider. The CIO coordinates the activities of the 
Consultant under general direction from the Investment Committee. In all cases, the Consultant and its 
representatives shall offer advice that is solely in the interest of OCERS and perform its duties in accordance 
with the OCERS’ investment guidelines. 
The firm selected as General Investment Consultant as a result of this RFP will provide Investment Policy 
advice, conduct asset allocation study, manage total portfolio risk, report and monitor the entire portfolio, 
conduct due diligence, collaborate with OCERS’ Investment Team and Investment Committee, and attend 
meetings as needed. 
The firm(s) selected as Private Equity, Real Assets, and/or Real Estate Investment Consultant(s) as a result of 
this RFP will provide strategic advice, source investments, conduct due diligence, report and monitor the 
alternative assets portfolio, collaborate with OCERS’ Investment Team and Investment Committee, and attend 
meetings as needed.

For purposes of this RFP, the asset class/ strategy coverages of consultant services are shown below.
Consultant Service Asset Classes/ Strategies
General Investments and Risk Global public equity, fixed income, credit (corporate credit, EM debt, 
opportunistic credit, and performing bond-like private credit), risk
mitigation (long-term treasuries, global macro, systematic trend

and private equity co-investments
Real Assets Energy, infrastructure, timber, and agriculture as well as co-investments
Real Estate Core and non-core real estate investments as well as co-investments
Note to respondents: OCERS has elected to define its credit exposure under two different asset classes - credit 
and private equity. 
The performing bond-like private credit funds in credit asset class, including but not limited to traditional 
sponsor-focused mezzanine and senior debt funds, seek to deliver predictable returns while protecting 
against losses. The dominant characteristics of the private credit in credit asset class are interest rate risk 
and credit risk. The bond-like private credit allocation is expected to be covered by the General 
Investment Consultant.
The non-performing and/or equity-like private credit funds in private equity asset class, including but not 
limited to levered direct lending and distressed debt, seek to generate more private equity-like returns. 
These strategies tend to have an element of equity optionality and the return is often driven by an 
illiquidity premium and complexity premium. The equity-like private credit allocation is expected to be
covered by the Private Equity Consultant.
OCERS has a Unique Strategy category for strategies that are differentiated from those in the portfolio’s other 
main asset classes. Given that these types of ideas can have characteristics of multiple or any asset class and 
market type, public or private, the investments in the Unique Strategy category can fall under the purview of 
any OCERS’ consultant. 
The detailed scope of services for this engagement is outlined in Scope of Services (Appendix “D”). 
Respondents are invited to submit proposals for any one, combination, or all of the Investments Consulting 
Services described above. The proposal must clearly identify the intended service offering(s) in Proposal Cover 
Page and Checklist (Appendix “B”). The proposal must demonstrate that the Respondent is capable of 
providing advice and recommendations on the types of assets identified in the Respondent’s proposal. 
Proposals must specifically identify the scope of services offered under appropriate descriptive headings and 
any investment asset categories, strategies, or vehicles excluded from the services offered. The initial term of 
the contract awarded pursuant to this RFP will be for a five (5) year period, with OCERS retaining the option to 
renew the contract for up to an additional one (1) year.

Asset Class Objective and Goals:
• Global Public Equity
The investment objective of the global equity is to achieve consistent positive real returns and to 
maximize long-term total return with prudent levels of risk through a combination of income and 
capital appreciation. OCERS has adopted a style diversified structure that is designed to have 
aggregate equity portfolio characteristics similar to that of the global equity market as represented by 
the MSCI ACWI IMI Index. While passive management is utilized in the more efficient parts of the 
markets, active management is favored for small cap, emerging market equity, etc.
• Private Equity
The objective of the private equity asset class is to provide diversification for the overall portfolio and 
enhance returns; a diversified global portfolio targeting top-quartile managers within each segment of 
the market. The asset class is composed of fund of funds, direct private equity, and non-performing 
and/or equity-like private credit. The asset class is targeting 63% buyout, 25% venture, 7% special 
situations, and 5% other (non-core interests through legacy FoFs); and 64% North America, 20% 
Europe, 13% Asia, and 3% Global. Additionally, 10% of the annual private equity commitments are set 
aside for co-investment opportunities alongside OCERS’ current existing GP relationships. 
OCERS will continue to seek out direct fund investments in top-quartile managers globally. Private 
equity has a pacing plan to deploy $675 million in 2021 and $700 million in 2022. OCERS will also focus 
on top-quartile managers that will provide co-investment opportunities, allowing OCERS to top up on 
“best ideas” while bringing down the total fee load. Co-investments with existing and approved 
General Partners in sizes of $5 to $10 million are approved under the current guidelines.
• Fixed Income
The objective of the fixed income asset class is to diversify equity risk, preserve capital, generate 
income, and in the case of TIPS, protect against inflation. The asset class is broken down into two main 
categories: investment grade bonds and TIPS. The former is mostly actively managed through core and 
core-plus mandates. TIPS are invested in an index fund. 
• Credit
The objective of this asset class is to allow the plan to capture the credit risk premium. Credit has a 7% 
overall target in the portfolio and includes four main sub-asset classes: corporate credit, opportunistic 
credit, emerging markets debt, and performing bond-like private credit. The asset class is targeting 
35% corporate credit and opportunistic credit, 29% emerging markets debt, and 36% private credit.
The corporate credit allocation is made up of corporate bonds and banks loans that are mainly below 
investment grade. Opportunistic credit seeks to deliver returns by taking advantage of periods of 
credit dislocation in public markets. OCERS’ emerging markets debt exposure is predominantly 
expressed through blended mandates in local and external emerging markets sovereign debt. Finally, 
the majority of the private credit exposure is in middle market direct lending and asset based lending.
As for the private credit sub-asset class, it has a pacing plan to deploy $125 to $200 million per year 
across 2 to 3 investments.
• Real Assets: 
The objective of the real assets asset class is to provide diversification for the overall portfolio while 
providing income and an inflation hedge. Real assets has a 5% overall target in the portfolio and 
includes infrastructure, energy, timber, agriculture, and other hard asset strategies. 
Real assets has a pacing plan to deploy $100 to $150 million per year across 2 to 3 investments.

Investment Consultant Services: Requests for Proposal 16 of 37
• Real Estate
Within real estate, OCERS targets 60% to core strategies and 40% to non-core strategies with up to 
10% of the real estate allocation permitted to be invested in non-U.S. assets. OCERS will continue to 
move towards a balance of core and non-core real estate investment allocations.
• Risk Mitigation
The objective of the risk mitigation asset class includes protecting against an equity market decline, 
diversifying the total portfolio away from growth risk, and having a positive return over a cycle. The 
asset class is composed of 25% target allocation each to long-term treasuries, global macro, 
systematic trend following, and alternative risk premia. 
• Unique Strategies
The objective of the unique strategies asset class is to enhance return and diversify the risks of the 
OCERS’ portfolio while exhibiting a low correlation to public equity and fixed income markets. This 
portion of the portfolio is reserved for strategies that are truly unique and while differentiated from 
those in the portfolio’s other main asset classes, can have characteristics of multiple or overlapping 
asset classes but are not easily categorized by just one in particular. For this reason, Unique Strategies 
may fall under the purview of any OCERS’ Investment Consultant.
Since there is no target for Unique Strategies, the category will continue to be utilized in an 
opportunistic manner and will continue to evolve over time, likely increasing the OCERS’ portfolio 
exposure to new and niche platforms and strategies in the future.

SECTION 2
SCOPE OF SERVICES
A. Background Information
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the Anchorage 
Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; AO No. 2000-
65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and fire employees hired July 1, 1968, or later retroactively 
became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans including a surplus benefit plan, all of 
which were created for the purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain 
in the service of the Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through 
the establishment of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and
their beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and Plan
III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994, for new command police and fire, July 
17, 1994, for union firefighters and all new union police officers October 5, 1994.
A nine-member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has sole and 
exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt delivery
of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and administration 
of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the Board and 
Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the primary
responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into the 
APFRS Plans. The Retirement System is also subject to an annual independent audit
commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial valuation and audit are provided
to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Municipal Assembly.

The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the 
following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment 
performance history.
F. Manager Guidelines:
1. Managers shall have full discretionary authority in the selection 
and retention of investments, subject to the provision of law, trust 
agreements, this Statement of Investment Policy as amended from 
time to time and investment management agreement between the 
System and the manager.
2. The responsibility for security selection shall lie with the managers.
The managers, however, shall operate within these investment 
guidelines which shall conform to applicable governmental 
regulations, and shall cover four specific areas: (a) diversification; 
(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.
a. Diversification:
(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the 
security’s weight in the agreed upon market index 
plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be 
requested as provided below in section (d).
(2) No security shall be bought unless it is traded on
one of the major security exchanges or the Over-The-Counter (OTC) market. Listed American
Depository Receipts (ADR’s) shall be an approved
investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a 
manager’s portfolio. The manager is required to provide
the Board with a list and explanation of the types of
derivatives they expect to invest in, the purposes for
holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a 
description of the risks associated with these 
investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

10
but individual issues must have a Flow Uncertainty
Index (“FLUX”) score of 15 or less.
b. Credit quality:
(1) Commercial paper must be rated P-1 and/or A-1 by
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s respectively.
(2) The total bond portfolio will maintain a minimum 
average credit rating of “BBB+” as rated by both 
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. For Purposes of
compliance with this Policy, the manager will 
adhere to the same ratings scale and policy as that 
employed by Bloomberg in the structure of the 
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (utilizing ratings by 
Moody’s, S & P and Fitch).
c. Portfolio Duration:
Total portfolio weighted average duration should not
exceed 120% of the bond market’s duration utilizing the
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index.
d. Restricted transactions:
(1) Conflict of interest and transactions between a
fiduciary and parties in interest, as described in
Sections 406 and 408 of Title I, Employee 
Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), are 
prohibited which provisions are adopted for use in 
this System.
(2) No transactions shall be made which might 
threaten the tax exempt status of the system.
(3) No letter stocks shall be purchased.
(4) No funds shall be borrowed.
(5) No short sales shall be made.
(6) No tax-exempt bond shall be purchased or retained
unless, on a comparable quality and duration basis, it
provides an expected return superior to that of a 
taxable bond.
(7) No private placements shall be purchased. 
However, Rule 144A securities with registration 
rights are permitted investments.
(8) No non-exchange-listed derivatives shall be
purchased or sold by any of the System’s managers.

11
e. Exceptions to Manager Guidelines:
(9) The Board acknowledges that when it is in the best
interests of the System to invest in a collective 
vehicle (i.e. comingled fund or mutual fund); it is 
not possible to dictate specific investment 
prohibitions. Therefore, it shall be the duty of the 
manager of such commingled fund to report to the 
Board on a periodic basis, the extent to which the 
investment strategies differ from the Board’s SIP.
Periodically, the Board will review the differences 
and determine if the commingled fund remains in 
the best interest of the System.
(10) The managers may request exceptions to the
restrictions outlined in V.F.2. by written
request to the Board.
(11) All exceptions will be submitted in writing to the
Board who will, after reviewing and receiving 
advice from the Fund’s Investment Consultant,
render a decision with regard to the request at the
next board meeting.
3. Brokerage Transactions
The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)
J. APPROVAL
This latest revision to the Statement of Investment Policy is approved by a super-majority vote of the Retirement Board at the meeting held on August 16, 2023.

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the 
following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment 
performance history.
F. Manager Guidelines:
1. Managers shall have full discretionary authority in the selection 
and retention of investments, subject to the provision of law, trust 
agreements, this Statement of Investment Policy as amended from 
time to time and investment management agreement between the 
System and the manager.
2. The responsibility for security selection shall lie with the managers.
The managers, however, shall operate within these investment 
guidelines which shall conform to applicable governmental 
regulations, and shall cover four specific areas: (a) diversification; 
(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.
a. Diversification:
(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the 
security’s weight in the agreed upon market index 
plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be 
requested as provided below in section (d).
(2) No security shall be bought unless it is traded on
one of the major security exchanges or the Over-The-Counter (OTC) market. Listed American
Depository Receipts (ADR’s) shall be an approved
investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a 
manager’s portfolio. The manager is required to provide
the Board with a list and explanation of the types of
derivatives they expect to invest in, the purposes for
holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a 
description of the risks associated with these 
investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

10
but individual issues must have a Flow Uncertainty
Index (“FLUX”) score of 15 or less.
b. Credit quality:
(1) Commercial paper must be rated P-1 and/or A-1 by
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s respectively.
(2) The total bond portfolio will maintain a minimum 
average credit rating of “BBB+” as rated by both 
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. For Purposes of
compliance with this Policy, the manager will 
adhere to the same ratings scale and policy as that 
employed by Bloomberg in the structure of the 
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (utilizing ratings by 
Moody’s, S & P and Fitch).
c. Portfolio Duration:
Total portfolio weighted average duration should not
exceed 120% of the bond market’s duration utilizing the
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index.
d. Restricted transactions:
(1) Conflict of interest and transactions between a
fiduciary and parties in interest, as described in
Sections 406 and 408 of Title I, Employee 
Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), are 
prohibited which provisions are adopted for use in 
this System.
(2) No transactions shall be made which might 
threaten the tax exempt status of the system.
(3) No letter stocks shall be purchased.
(4) No funds shall be borrowed.
(5) No short sales shall be made.
(6) No tax-exempt bond shall be purchased or retained
unless, on a comparable quality and duration basis, it
provides an expected return superior to that of a 
taxable bond.
(7) No private placements shall be purchased. 
However, Rule 144A securities with registration 
rights are permitted investments.
(8) No non-exchange-listed derivatives shall be
purchased or sold by any of the System’s managers.

11
e. Exceptions to Manager Guidelines:
(9) The Board acknowledges that when it is in the best
interests of the System to invest in a collective 
vehicle (i.e. comingled fund or mutual fund); it is 
not possible to dictate specific investment 
prohibitions. Therefore, it shall be the duty of the 
manager of such commingled fund to report to the 
Board on a periodic basis, the extent to which the 
investment strategies differ from the Board’s SIP.
Periodically, the Board will review the differences 
and determine if the commingled fund remains in 
the best interest of the System.
(10) The managers may request exceptions to the
restrictions outlined in V.F.2. by written
request to the Board.
(11) All exceptions will be submitted in writing to the
Board who will, after reviewing and receiving 
advice from the Fund’s Investment Consultant,
render a decision with regard to the request at the
next board meeting.
3. Brokerage Transactions
The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)
J. APPROVAL
This latest revision to the Statement of Investment Policy is approved by a super-majority vote of the Retirement Board at the meeting held on August 16, 2023.
